transcript.content: Right, let's get into it. I want to ask about somewhere a bit more specific. Think about where you actually spend time with your male friends — not just a general area, but a particular place, maybe somewhere you go back to regularly. What's that spot for you, and what is it about that place that makes it the one?

For me it's probably just the pub, to be honest. There's one near where I work — couple of mates from work go there regular, so you end up there after a shift or whatever. Nothing fancy about it. Just, I dunno, it's there, it's familiar, the lads know the staff. You don't have to think about it too much. We might grab some food there sometimes, bit of standard pub fare really, but that's not really the draw if I'm being honest. It's more just the spot where you know you'll bump into people you know. Cheaper than going somewhere posher as well, I reckon.

Yeah, I mean I've got a couple of spots like that down here too — you know, places you just default to. But I think it's a bit different in London, right? There's so many places it's almost overwhelming sometimes. Like, you could go literally anywhere, but because of that you end up just sticking with the one you know works. There's more competition, more options, but somehow that makes the familiar spot even more valuable in a weird way. You know what I mean?

With mates I've got this bar we go to fairly regularly — it's not the cheapest, not the fanciest, but it's sort of become the default because, I dunno, once you've got a place where everyone knows the vibe and the staff actually know what you're drinking, you just go back. You're not constantly trying to figure out where to go next.

Yeah, that makes sense actually. It's like — Birmingham's got loads of places too, especially city centre, right? And you'd think with all that choice you'd be trying different spots all the time, but it's the opposite. You end up at the same place because at least you know what you're getting. It's not really about it being cheap or convenient, it's more like... you don't have to negotiate it every time, you know? Like, you text the lads and say the pub, and everyone just knows. No one's going to argue about it. Whereas if you start suggesting a different place every week you're just making it harder, aren't you? The familiar spot becomes like the thing that holds it together a bit.

Yeah, exactly. It's more than just not having to think about it though, isn't it? There's something about... I don't know, you trust it. You trust the place, you trust that the people you go with will be there, you trust that it'll be alright. Like, when you go somewhere new you've got all this stuff in your head — is it going to be weird, are the lads actually going to like it, is it going to be awkward. But when you've got your spot, you just know. It's familiar.

I think that's why even though there's loads of places round here, people do stick with one. It's not really about efficiency, or at least not just that. It's more like... belonging, I suppose. You belong there a bit. The staff know you, the other regulars know you. That matters more than having endless options, if I'm honest.

Connor's picked up on something there — that it's less about the place itself and more about trust, knowing you belong there. Does that ring true for any of you? Sam, Noah, Bilal — what's your version of that?

Yeah, I get what Connor's saying. I've got a spot too — there's a curry house not far from where I live, been going there for years now. The owner knows me, knows what I usually order, we chat a bit. But it's different from what Henry and Connor are describing, I think. Like, yeah, it's familiar and I trust it, but I don't really need the staff to know me, or for it to be about belonging in that way. It's more just... I can go in and not have to explain myself, you know? I'm not performing anything. With mates it might be different, but on my own it's just nice to sit down and not have to think about whether I'm going to fit in or anything like that. The place just lets me be. Maybe that's what belonging means round here though, different from London or whatever.

That's fair, yeah. I think you're onto something different there actually. Like, what you're describing with the curry house — that's not about the social thing, it's more about just... being able to exist without having to manage anything. That's valid.

Round here I suppose you get both, depending. Like with the lads it's definitely about the recognition, the social glue thing we were talking about. But there's places I go on my own, coffee spots or whatever, where it's more like what you're saying. You just want to be left alone basically, not have to think about it. Though I guess even then, if you go to the same place regularly, you do end up with a bit of that familiarity. The barista knows your order.

But you're right — it's not the same thing as needing to belong in a group. Sometimes you just want to not be visible, kind of. Not performing. That's a different reason to keep going back to the same place, isn't it?

That's a useful distinction actually — the place you go with the lads versus the place you go just to not have to think. Right, let's shift slightly. Still thinking about your everyday lives — how do you actually decide what to eat? Day to day, what shapes that?

Yeah, I mean for me it's pretty straightforward really. What's in the house, what I can be bothered to make, or if I'm out of time then it's just whatever's quickest. I don't really think about it that much to be honest.

Living out where I am, there's not loads of options anyway, so you kind of work with what you've got. If I'm grabbing something with mates it's usually just the same few spots we know work — chippy, the local, whatever. But day to day when I'm just eating at home, it's more about what my wife's got on the go, or if she's made something, or I'll just throw together whatever's there.

I get what you lot were saying about the familiar places and belonging and that, but I don't know — I think for me personally it's less about all that when it comes to food, and more just about... does it work, is it there, will it fill me up. Maybe I'm just not thinking about it as much as you lot.

Yeah, but that's exactly what I mean though, Noah. Like, you're not thinking about it, right? But you're still ending up at the same spots — the chippy, the local. That's the default kicking in, isn't it? Even when you're just trying to be practical about it, you're still defaulting to what's already there and what you know works.

I think that's actually the same thing Connor and Bilal were saying, just from a different angle. Like, Connor's talking about belonging and trust with his mates, Bilal's talking about not having to perform at the curry house — but Noah, what you're doing is just as much a default. You're not choosing between ten options, you're just going to the chippy because it's there and it does the job. Same mechanism, just... you're not thinking about the social side of it, but you're still stuck in the pattern.

I reckon that's what happens round here in the suburbs. There's not enough choice to make you think about it differently anyway. So whether you care about the belonging bit or you just want something quick, you end up in the same places. It's easier not to look around.

Nah, but that's not the same thing though, is it? I'm not stuck in a pattern — there literally isn't much else round here. If I want food I've got the chippy, I've got a couple of takeaways, maybe a pub or two. That's it. It's not that I'm defaulting because I haven't thought about it, it's that there's nothing else to choose from.

Like, you're in the suburbs too, Sam, but you're sort of acting like it's a choice thing — like, oh, we're just stuck in patterns because we're not thinking. But for me it's just practical. If there was a proper Thai place or a decent Italian round the corner I'd probably go there sometimes. But there isn't, so I go to the chippy. That's not me being stuck, that's just... that's what's available.

Connor's talking about loads of options in London and still picking the same bar — that's different, that's actually a choice. Mine's just, there's two or three places that exist and one of them does decent chips. I don't really see how that's the same mechanism.

Fair point actually, yeah. You're right — that is different. I wasn't thinking about it like that. Like, Connor's got actual choice and he's choosing to stick with the same place anyway, whereas you've just got the chippy because that's what's there. That's not the same thing at all really.

I guess where I live there's a bit more than your area maybe, but you're still right — it's not like I'm weighing up loads of options every time I fancy a takeaway. There's probably three or four places that actually exist within reach, and yeah, I just go to one of them. But I wasn't really thinking about whether that's a choice or just... what's available, you know? You've made a fair point there.

Yeah, that distinction between 'I'm choosing not to think about it' and 'there's just not much there' is actually a useful one. Okay — let's shift direction a bit. So far we've been talking about where you eat and how you end up there. I want to move into something a bit different. Do you think your gender — being a man — influences what you eat? Either day to day or in certain situations. Anyone want to kick off?

Yeah, I think it does actually. Not in a massive way necessarily, but... like, there are certain things you just don't order when you're with mates, aren't there? I mean, I'll go to the curry house on my own and get what I want, but if I'm out with lads and we're at the pub or wherever, you're sort of aware of what people might think. Not that anyone's going to say anything, but you know what I mean.

Like, you're not ordering a salad or something that might look... I dunno, too careful or whatever. You just get the burger or the pie or the chips. It's not a conscious thing most of the time, it's just what you do. But then when I'm on my own at the curry house, I can get whatever — rice, veg, whatever — and no one's watching it, so it doesn't matter.

I think it's more about not wanting to stand out or have it be a thing, to be honest. You just want to blend in with what the other lads are doing.

Yeah, I know what you mean. Though I'd say for me it's changed a bit over the years, to be honest. When I was younger — like, in my twenties — I definitely did that. You'd be aware of it, wouldn't you? You wouldn't order certain things because it felt like it'd make you look a certain way. But now I'm 35, I just... I order what I want. If I fancy a salad or whatever, I'll get it. The lads don't care, and if they did, I'm not bothered anymore.

But yeah, I remember that thing you're talking about though. You're not thinking about it consciously, it's just built in — like, you know what's acceptable to order with mates and what isn't. It's a bit mad when you think about it, isn't it? Like, why would anyone care what another bloke eats. But it's definitely there when you're younger. I think you grow out of it a bit though. Or at least, I have.

Yeah, I hear you on that Henry. I'm 32 now, so I'm kind of in between I think. Like, I'm not as worried about it as I probably was in my twenties, but it's still there sometimes depending on who I'm with, you know? 

It's not like I'm rigidly avoiding things anymore, but there's certain situations where I'll still just go with what feels... I dunno, neutral. Safe. Especially if it's lads I don't know that well, or work people or whatever. But then with the ones I've known for ages, or when I'm just doing my own thing, it doesn't really matter.

I think it's more about context than age maybe. Like, the curry house thing I mentioned — that's me being myself because I'm on my own and it's my space. But yeah, there's definitely still that awareness when you're with a group. I reckon I could probably care less about it if I tried, but you don't really think about it enough to challenge it, do you? It's just easier to fit in.

That's fair, yeah. Maybe it's not just about age then. Like, I said I don't care anymore, but that's probably because I've known the same lads for years, you know? So it's not even a thing. But if I was going out with work people I didn't know well, or someone new's joined the group, I might still do it without even realizing. You're right about that — context matters more than just how old you are.

It's a bit like what you said though, about not really thinking about it enough to challenge it. Like, once you get comfortable in a situation, you stop noticing you're doing it. So it's not that I've gone, "Right, I'm older now, I'm going to order what I want." It's more that the situation's just... easy. Low stakes. No one's judging because we all know each other properly. 

But I reckon if you put me somewhere unfamiliar with new faces, I'd probably slip back into that a bit, without thinking. You'd just go for the safe option again, wouldn't you?

Yeah, but that's the thing though, isn't it? I mean, you can notice it if you want to. Like, you're saying you'd slip back into it without thinking, but you could just... not, couldn't you? Even with new people.

I get what you mean about the comfortable situations — that's different, that's just being relaxed. But the unfamiliar stuff, the new faces — I think at 32 you know enough about yourself to make a choice rather than just defaulting. You don't have to slip back into anything.

I'm not saying I always do it, but sometimes I'll just order what I actually want even if I don't know the people that well, and honestly? No one gives a shit. The world doesn't collapse. But the thing is, I have to actually decide to do it. It's easier not to. It's easier to just go for the safe burger like everyone else and not have it be a thing. But then you're just kind of... letting the situation run you, aren't you? Rather than just being who you are.

I think maybe it's worth noticing it, at least. That's different from obsessing over it, but just... knowing you're doing it, I mean.
Bilal, that's interesting — 'no one gives a shit.' Connor, Sam, Noah — does that match what you've found? Or are there situations where it actually does become a thing?

I mean... yeah, Bilal, intellectually I know no one gives a shit what I order. And obviously that's true, right? But it's not quite as simple as just deciding to do it, is it?

Like, I've done the thing where you're with work people or mates you don't know that well yet, and you tell yourself it doesn't matter, and you know logically it doesn't. But there's still that moment when you're looking at the menu and you think about it, you know? It's not like knowing it doesn't matter makes the awareness go away. The awareness is still there, even if you override it.

And maybe that's just me being a bit mental about it, but I think it's different in the suburbs actually. Like, where I live there's not loads of places, so you see the same people. You go to the same chippy, the same couple of pubs. You're not anonymous. So when you do something that's a bit different or stands out, it feels like... more people are noticing, even if they're not. There's fewer eyes around so when you break the pattern it somehow feels more visible.

I reckon it's easier to just fit in where you are because you know you're going to see the same people again. That's probably more of a factor for me than age or knowing myself better. It's just easier not to bother with it.

No, yeah, that's fair actually. I was being a bit... I dunno, simplistic maybe. You're right that knowing it doesn't matter doesn't make the feeling go away. That's true.

And the thing about the suburbs and seeing the same people — I get that. It's similar where I am in the urban bit here. It's not massive, you know? It's not like London where you're completely anonymous. You do see the same faces. The owner of the curry house knows me. You bump into people you know at the shops or whatever. So there's this awareness that if you're doing something different, it registers. Even if no one's actually bothered by it.

I think I was maybe talking about it too much like it's just a choice you make, like you can logic your way out of it. But actually it's more... embedded than that, isn't it? It's not really about being mentally weak or whatever. It's just how you're shaped by where you are and who you see regularly. The awareness doesn't just disappear because you turn 32 and know better.

I still think it's worth noticing it though. But yeah, you're right — noticing it and actually changing what you do are different things. The feeling's still there even when you know it shouldn't be.

That's a useful distinction — noticing it versus actually changing what you do. Sticking with that for a moment: are there particular foods you'd all associate with being more male or more female? Like, are there things that would feel out of place for a man to order, or things that are just... expected?

I mean, yeah — salads, definitely. That's the obvious one everyone mentions. Like, a big green salad with like, dressing on it, that feels coded as a bit feminine or like you're being careful or whatever. Same with anything that's got loads of veg in it, or anything that looks small or delicate, I suppose.

But in London it's a bit different I reckon. Like, there's so many people doing different things that it's harder for any one food to feel totally gendered. You see blokes eating all sorts of stuff. But even saying that, I know what you mean — there's still that awareness. Like, a burger, steak, chips, that's the safe zone. Anything that looks too health-conscious or fussy, you notice it more.

I think the thing is, even in London where there's loads of choice and loads of people, you still default to what feels like it won't be a thing. Because it's easier, innit? It's not about logic — I know full well no one cares. But there's this automatic thing where you just go for what feels neutral. Safe. And certain foods feel more neutral than others depending on whether they're kind of... I dunno, masculine-coded or whatever.

With the lads I've known for years it's different, like Henry said. But if I'm somewhere new or with people I don't know that well, I'd probably do the same as what you lot are describing. Just order something that blends in.

I mean, yeah, there's definitely stuff that's more coded one way or another. Like, you see salad and you think... I dunno, that's more of a woman thing or whatever. But honestly, I'm not sure it affects me that much day to day.

Like, I go to the chippy — you're getting chips, a burger, that's it. Not really thinking about whether it's masculine enough or whatever. It's just what's there, what fills you up. And when I'm at home I'll eat whatever my wife's made, so it's not really my choice anyway half the time. And if I'm grabbing something quick it's just... whatever works.

I think maybe it's different where you lot are with more options and more people around, you know? Like Sam was saying about the suburbs and seeing the same people — I get that. But I don't know, for me it's more just that there's one or two things available so you're not really deliberating about it enough to worry about what it looks like. The awareness just isn't there as much, I reckon.

I'm not sure I'd call myself out for ordering something that felt a bit off if I actually wanted it. But then, the options where I am mean that's kind of a moot point. I'm not going to the chippy and going "is this masculine enough?" I'm just getting chips.

Thanks Noah. So across the group there's something pretty consistent here — that awareness around what you order is real, it's context-dependent, and knowing it's there doesn't just switch it off. Right, I want to shift us to something a bit more hypothetical. Imagine you actually decided to go plant-based — like, properly, cutting out meat. What would need to change in your life for that to actually work?

God, that's... yeah, I don't know. A lot, probably.

I mean, my wife does most of the cooking at home, so it wouldn't just be me deciding that, would it? That'd be a conversation with her. And I think she'd probably think I was mad to be honest. Like, we're just... we eat meat. That's what we do. Chicken, beef, whatever's on offer at Tesco. That's normal for us.

If I actually went plant-based I'd probably have to cook a lot more of my own stuff, because I'm not going to ask her to completely change how she cooks for the whole family. And that's... I don't know, that feels like a lot of effort. I work, she works, we've got the house to sort. I'm not going to spend my evenings researching vegan recipes or whatever.

And then socially, right — going to the pub with the lads, or the chippy. What am I ordering then? They're not really set up for that where I am. The chippy does chips, that's about it. You'd have to be the weird one, wouldn't you? The bloke who's only eating chips because he's plant-based. 

I think if my wife was into it and we were both doing it together, maybe that'd be different. But on my own? Nah, I don't see it happening to be honest.

Yeah but I mean — and I don't mean this as a dig at you Noah — but some of that's just accepting the constraint as like, immovable, isn't it?

Like, you're saying your wife would think you were mad, and maybe she would. But that's a conversation you could have, you know? It's not like she'd say no and that's the end of it. And the cooking thing — loads of plant-based stuff is actually dead simple. It's not like you need to research recipes every night. You just... eat different stuff. Rice, beans, veg. My mate's vegetarian and he just eats normal food, just without the meat. He's not spending hours on it.

And the pub thing — I get that it's easier where you are with fewer options. But even in London where there's loads of places, you've still got the awareness thing we were talking about. You're still kind of defaulting to what feels safe. So it's not really about what's available, it's more about... you'd have to actually want to do it enough to deal with being a bit different about it.

I'm not saying it's easy or anything. But I think there's a difference between "it's genuinely impossible" and "it would require me to change some stuff and have some conversations and probably feel a bit uncomfortable." Those aren't the same thing, are they?

No yeah, fair enough. You're right, I could have a conversation with her about it. I'm not saying she'd shut it down completely or anything. I just... I don't know, it's not something that's on the table for us, really. It's not like I'm desperate to go plant-based and I'm just making excuses. I'm not. I like eating meat. I'm fine with how things are.

But you've got a point about accepting stuff as immovable when maybe it's not, I suppose. Like, if I actually wanted to change something, I probably could. Have the conversation, work it out. But that's different from saying "I'm going to do this," isn't it? 

The thing is though, Connor — and I know you're not having a dig — but it's easier to say that when you're in London with loads of options and loads of people doing different things. Where I am, if I started going to the chippy ordering chips and beans or whatever because I'd gone plant-based, people would notice. It's just different. It's not impossible, you're right. But it would genuinely feel like more of a thing, just because of where I live and who I see regularly.

I'm not saying I'm trapped or whatever. But I think there's a real difference between "you could do this if you wanted" and "this would actually fit into my life as it is." For me right now, it doesn't. And I'm okay with that, to be honest.

Yeah, okay, that's fair actually. I was maybe being a bit... I dunno, preachy about it. You're right — there's a difference between something being possible and it actually fitting into how you live, isn't there?

Like, I get what you're saying about where you are and people noticing. That's real. And the thing is, if you're not actually wanting to do it in the first place, then yeah — all that extra stuff, the conversations, people clocking it, it's just not worth the hassle for something you're not bothered about anyway.

I think I was kind of assuming there was this thing you wanted but were just making excuses about. But you're just saying you don't actually want to, really. And you're okay with that. That's fair enough, innit.

I suppose where I am it might feel different because there's so much choice and so many people doing different things that it's easier to just... do your thing without it being this whole statement about it. But that doesn't make your point wrong. If something doesn't fit your life, it doesn't fit. You're not going to force it just to prove you could.

Yeah, cheers. I mean, I wasn't trying to sound like I'm stuck or anything. I'm genuinely just... I eat meat, it works for me, my wife cooks it most nights, we're all fine with it. That's just how it is.

I think the thing is, I'm not sat around wishing I could do something different and feeling held back, you know? Like, I'm not secretly wanting to go plant-based and making excuses about it. I'm just not interested in it. So all those constraints — the wife, the options round here, what people would think — they're not really constraints then, are they? They're just... context for a life I'm already happy with.

Whereas what you were saying earlier about ordering a salad in London — that sounds like something you might actually want to do, but you're aware of it so you don't. That's different. That's an actual constraint on something you want.

For me it's more just that the question doesn't really apply. I'm not wanting to change what I eat. So yeah, I could have conversations and change things around, but why would I? There's no pull toward it.

That's a useful distinction Noah — between something holding you back from what you want, versus it just not being something you want in the first place. What about the rest of you? Sam, Henry, Bilal — if you think about that same question, what would actually need to change for you to go plant-based, where do you land on it?

I mean, honestly — for me it's not really something I'm thinking about either. Like, I eat meat, it's what I've always done. I don't think I'd want to go fully plant-based.

But I think for me it'd be different from Noah in a way. Like, I could probably do it if I actually decided I wanted to. I'm 35, I can cook for myself, I don't have someone else doing the meals. So the practical stuff — that's fine, I could figure it out.

The thing is though, it's the whole setup, isn't it? Like, the pub I go to — what am I ordering there? You'd be the one guy eating something different. And at work, if you're getting lunch with people, it becomes this thing. You become the plant-based guy. And I know, I know — it shouldn't matter, we've talked about all that. But it does in practice.

I think what would actually need to change isn't just the food itself, it's more... you'd need everyone around you to shift with you, or at least enough of them to not make it weird. Or you'd have to care less about standing out than you currently do. And I don't know if that changes just because you get older. I'm fine with ordering what I want now, but that's different from being the one person doing something noticeably different in a familiar group of people.

So yeah, I could do it practically. But the whole social landscape of it — that's what would actually need to shift, I reckon.

Henry, something you said is sticking with me. Earlier you said the lads don't care and if they did you're not bothered anymore — like that social awareness had kind of faded. But just now you're saying the whole social landscape would need to shift for you to actually do this, because you'd be the one person doing something noticeably different in a familiar group. How do those two things sit together for you?

Yeah, fair point. That's... I don't know, that's a good catch actually.

I think there's a difference though, isn't there? Like, when I'm at the pub with the lads and I order a salad or whatever, they know me. They know I'm just ordering what I want that day. It's not a statement about who I am or anything. They're not going to think I've had some big ideological shift or whatever. It's just Henry ordering a salad.

But going plant-based is different, isn't it? That's not just one meal, that's a whole... change. And then every time you're out, every time you're ordering something, it's this visible thing. You're not just being yourself, you're being the one who's made this choice and everyone's aware of it. That's different from just not caring what people think about one meal.

I know that sounds like I'm contradicting myself a bit. But I think one's about just not overthinking a single choice, and the other's about being willing to be visibly different in an ongoing way. Those feel like different levels, to me. Does that make sense, or am I just... talking myself round it?

No, that distinction makes sense — one meal is just a meal, a whole shift is something people read differently. Sam, Bilal — you've not weighed in on this one yet. Same question: what would actually need to change for either of you to go plant-based?

I think... I'm somewhere in between actually. Like, I'm not desperate to go plant-based or anything. I eat meat, it's normal. But I don't think I'd be completely closed to it either, if there was a reason to do it.

The thing is though — and Henry's kind of got at this — it's not really about the practical stuff for me. Like, I can cook. I know what plant-based food is. That's fine. It's more about... what it would mean socially, I guess. Like, at the curry house on my own, I could order whatever I wanted and it wouldn't be a thing. That's my space.

But with mates, or at work, or just around — it would become a thing, wouldn't it? And not because people would be horrible about it, but because it's visible. It's a shift. And I think what Henry said about it being different from just ordering a salad once — that's true. That's just a meal. But if you're doing it all the time, then you're the plant-based guy. That's different.

So what would need to change? I dunno, maybe if more people around me were doing it, it wouldn't feel like such a statement about who you are. Or if I actually had a strong reason to do it — like, genuinely cared about it for environmental or health reasons or something. But just deciding to do it randomly? That feels harder than Henry's making it sound, if I'm being honest. Not impossible, but harder.
Sam, you've been quiet on this one — where do you land on it?

Yeah, I mean... I think I'm a bit like Bilal actually. I'm not desperate to go plant-based or anything, but I'm not completely against the idea either. It's not like it's unthinkable, you know?

But I think what Henry and Bilal are saying about it becoming a thing — that's the bit that sits with me. Where I live, if you start doing something noticeably different, it registers.
